newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary '97 budget may boost cool economy - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary '97 budget may boost cool economy - analysts.

text.p: Hungary's 1997 budget, approved by the Parliament on Tuesday, continues the past two years' strict fiscal course but may give more ground for economic growth, analysts and politicians said.

The question is if the measures aiming at faster growth will be sufficient to boost the economy, which was cooled by the austerity programme launched in 1995 aimed at cutting soaring budget and current account deficits, they added.
"Next year will be decisive," Mihaly Varga of the opposition party Fidesz told Reuters. "We will see if the restrictions of the past years made sense and economic growth begins or not."

The one-chamber Parliament, where the ruling Socialist-Liberal coalition holds 278 of the 386 seats, approved the 1997 central state budget law with 257 votes in favour, 80 against and two abstentions.

The planned deficit of the general government budget, including social security, is 392 billion forints ($2.40 billion) ($2.40 billion) or 4.9 percent of GDP, up from the four percent target for 1996.
The rise is mainly due to changes, called technical by the government and most analysts, in the accounting of state debt.
According to the government forecast, Hungary's GDP will be around 7,960 billion forints next year.
The government forecasts that the growth rate of the gross domestic product (GDP) will rise to two to three percent next year from the less than one percent increase expected for 1996.

The new law is seen as less tough for ordinary Hungarians than the 1995 and 1996 budgets as according to the government's plans real wages will maintain their real value in 1997, compared with a total drop of some 15 percent in 1995 and 1996.
"One of the most important factors from the point of view of GDP (gross domestic product) growth is that real wages will not drop further," Budapest Bank analyst Peter Bihari said.

Finance Ministry Deputy Secretary of State Csaba Laszlo told Reuters that economic growth would also be encouraged by corporate taxation changes, measures cutting personal income tax by 1.5 percent in 1997 and the planned abolishment of the six percent import duty surcharge in the first half of 1997.

The average of the expectations of 10 analysts in a recent Reuters poll for 1997 GDP growth was 2.39 percent, compared with 0.63 for 1996, while the analysts said next year's budget deficit would be between 310 and 380 billion forints.
However, some analysts said the 1997 economic policies lacked long-awaited and necessary measures for the reform of the pension, health care, education and administration systems.

"The problem is not with the budget, but with the fact that the long-term processes of budget reform are still not planned," said GKI Research Institute Managing Director Gabor Papanek. "They abolish hospital beds one week, and next week they put them back in the hospitals."
The central state budget is one of the two major components of the general government budget, the other being the social security budget, which parliament is expected to pass on Thursday.

The planned 1997 deficit of the social security sector is 13 billion forints. Analysts said the deficit may exceed the target substantially as the changes in the rules of social security contributions may not bring the expected result.

However, the general government deficit is likely to be around the target and next year's economic developments will probably help Hungary gett closer to meeting European Union monetary criteria for membership, analysts said.
"In this sense Hungarians do not have more problems than some of the EU members," Papanek said.
However, inflation in 1997 will remain still well above the EMU's maastricht criteria, which is currently around three percent, though the decline of inflation is seen as continuing.

The analyst poll showed that inflation was expected to drop to some 23.6 percent in 1996 from 28.2 in 1997, and further decrease to some 19 percent in 1997, compared with the government target of 17-18 percent. ($1=163.55 Forint)
